titre: The Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum Theft
accroche: On the night of March 18, 1990, two fake police officers walk out with thirteen works. None has ever been recovered.
contenu_vulgarise:
Boston, the night of March 18, 1990. Two men in police uniforms ring the intercom of the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum and say they are responding to a disturbance call. The night guard breaks protocol: he lets them in through the employee entrance. It is they, not the guards, who will soon be giving the orders.

## Eighty-One Minutes

The two men handcuff the two guards and take them to the basement, where they restrain them. Motion detectors record the thieves' movements toward the galleries, where they spend eighty-one minutes. In the Dutch Room, they cut out of their frames Rembrandt's *Christ in the Storm on the Sea of Galilee*, his only seascape according to the museum's security director, and *A Lady and Gentleman in Black*, by the same painter. They also remove Vermeer's *The Concert* and a *Landscape with an Obelisk* by Govaert Flinck from their frames, lift an ancient Chinese bronze ritual vessel, and take a small Rembrandt etching, a self-portrait. In the Short Gallery, they take five works by Degas and a bronze eagle from the Napoleonic era. On the ground floor, in the Blue Room, they take Manet's *Chez Tortoni* (*At Tortoni's*), whose frame is also left behind. The thieves leave at 2:45 a.m., in two trips to their car. The guards remain handcuffed until the police arrive at 8:15 a.m.

Thirteen works in all, valued at more than $500 million at the time: the FBI calls it the largest property crime in U.S. history. More than thirty-five years later, none has been recovered. The investigation remains open: the FBI, with the museum and the Massachusetts U.S. Attorney's Office, is following leads around the world, and, according to the FBI, the museum still offers up to ten million dollars for the return of the works in good condition.

## What the Empty Frames Say

Isabella Stewart Gardner died in 1924, and her will asks that her collection be exhibited permanently for the education and enjoyment of the public, according to her vision and taste. The museum draws a rule of conduct from this, which its director of conservation, Holly Salmon, sums up this way: it adds nothing, sells nothing, rearranges nothing, and that is why the loss of these works weighs so heavily. She adds: "We won't replace them. We are just waiting for them to come back." The museum will therefore not fill the gaps with anything else.

The frames, for their part, have stayed on the walls. They are not a trace of the theft left exactly as it was: according to the FBI, the museum decided in 1994, four years after the theft, to display them empty, a deliberate choice meant to recall what was lost and to express hope for a return. CBS Boston, for its part, ties the current state of the galleries to a passage in Gardner's will. Conservators have since repaired the five frames and put them back on the wall as placeholders, in the hope that the stolen paintings will one day take their places again.

The nuance shifts the question. The empty frames are not an absence someone forgot to fill; they are a gesture by the museum: to keep displaying a loss rather than close it over, so that the room remains, in the meantime, a place where these works belong.

carte.punch: Two fake police officers, a guard who breaks protocol, thirteen works gone in 81 minutes.
carte.idee: On the night of March 18, 1990, two men disguised as police officers steal thirteen works from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston, including a Vermeer and Rembrandts. Valued at more than $500 million at the time, none has been recovered.

quiz.question: Why does the Gardner Museum display empty frames in place of the stolen works?
choix: To keep the scene of the theft intact, at the FBI's request, untouched since 1990
Because copies of the stolen works hang there while the originals are awaited
To display the loss and the hope of a return: the museum decided this in 1994 and restored the frames as placeholders
Because the museum plans to fill them soon with replacement works
quiz.explication: According to the FBI, the museum decided in 1994 to display the empty frames, a deliberate choice to recall the loss and the hope of a return; it then repaired them and put them back on the wall as placeholders. They are not left as they were at the time of the theft, they hold no copies, and Holly Salmon says the museum will not replace the works: it is waiting for them to come back.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How long do the two thieves spend in the museum, and how many works do they take?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The two men spend eighty-one minutes in the museum and leave with thirteen works, taken from the Dutch Room, the Short Gallery, and the Blue Room.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which of these works was not stolen on the night of March 18, 1990?
choix: The Starry Night, by Van Gogh
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The thirteen stolen works are: Vermeer's The Concert, Manet's Chez Tortoni, five works by Degas, three works by Rembrandt, a landscape by Flinck, a Chinese ritual vessel, and a bronze eagle. The Starry Night is not among them.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the museum's director of conservation, Holly Salmon, sum up the rule the museum follows?
choix: It replaces every stolen work with a high-quality copy
It adds nothing, sells nothing and rearranges nothing, and will not replace the stolen works
It sells the empty frames to fund the reward
It closes the room until the works have been recovered
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to CBS Boston, Holly Salmon explains that the museum adds nothing, sells nothing and rearranges nothing, and that it will not replace the works: it is waiting for them to come back.
